topic: The Ghost Story Competition That Created Frankenstein

text.content: In the summer of 1816, a group of young, intelligent friends decided to take a long vacation near a beautiful lake in Switzerland. Unfortunately, the weather was absolutely terrible. A massive volcano had erupted in Asia, filling the sky with dark ash and causing freezing rain to fall across Europe. Because they were trapped inside their large house by the dark, stormy weather, the friends became very bored.

To entertain themselves, the group began reading old German ghost stories by the fire. After reading several books, one of the men suggested that they play a creative game. He challenged everyone in the room to write their own original, terrifying ghost story. The famous writer who originally challenged the group to this scary writing competition was a British poet. His name was Lord Byron.

One of the people in the house was an eighteen-year-old girl. For several days, she struggled to think of a scary idea for the competition. One night, while trying to sleep, she had a terrible, vivid nightmare. She dreamed about a pale student of science kneeling beside a horrible, stitched-together creature that had suddenly come to life. The young female author who experienced this famous nightmare was Mary Shelley.

When she woke up, she quickly began writing her story. She wrote about an ambitious young doctor who steals body parts from graveyards to build a living giant. While many people today mistakenly believe that the monster itself is named Frankenstein, this is incorrect. The name of the ambitious young scientist who actually created the monster in the book is Victor Frankenstein.

The story was eventually published as a full book in 1818, and it became a massive success. Readers were terrified by the idea that human science could go too far and create something dangerous. Because it combined modern scientific ideas with a fictional horror story, many modern experts consider Mary Shelley's book to be the very first science fiction novel ever written.
